Outlier Watch

Riverhead's 19 town funds, each checked against its own budget the year before, from 2020 to the 2027 Preliminary. A flag marks a swing large enough to be worth a second look. It is not proof of a problem, but a place to start asking questions.

Independent, unofficial project·Data last refreshed November 11, 2026·Recently refreshed·See data update details →
The line figures on this page are the Supervisor’s Tentative.

The Town Board’s six October 20, 2026 amendments changed 32 account lines in the Preliminary Budget. This page measures the Tentative as it was filed, so those changes are not in its figures. The funds, revenue and Budget Accuracy pages use the Preliminary.

Read the six amendments and their sources

In plain English

Across 133 fund-year comparisons from 2020 to the 2027 Preliminary, 7 clear the bar for a flag, one of them in the 2027 Preliminary.
  • What counts as an outlier: a fund whose appropriation moved at least 20% and at least $100,000 from one budget to the next: each adopted budget against the one before it, and the 2027 Preliminary against the 2026 adopted budget.
  • Why two thresholds: percent alone flags small funds swinging on a tiny base (a $15,000 fund going to $25,000 is "+67%" but immaterial); dollars alone would flag the General Fund almost every year simply because it is the biggest fund.
  • The 2027 Preliminary is a proposal: it is the Tentative with the Board's changes, the version the public hearing is held on. The Board adopts the 2027 budget by November 20.
  • What it does not mean: a flag is not an accusation. Big swings often have ordinary explanations — a bond payoff, a new contract, a one-time grant. Treat this as a starting point for a question at a Town Board meeting, not a conclusion.

Debt Service Fund, 2026 → 2027 Preliminary

What the 2027 Preliminary flags

Against the 2026 adopted budget, one fund moves past both bars: the Debt Service Fund, from $6,888,150 to $2,594,028 (−$4,294,122, −62.3%).

Five other funds change by $100,000 or more but by less than 20%, so they are not flagged: General Fund (up $2,818,911, 4.1%), Water District (up $393,684, 3.6%), Highway Fund (up $366,792, 4.6%), Riverhead Sewer District (up $268,816, 3.3%) and Riverhead Scavenger Waste (up $175,166, 7.8%).

One fund changes by 20% or more but by less than $100,000, so it is not flagged either: Calverton Parks Community Development Agency (up $31,161, 70.7%).

Why the Debt Service Fund falls

The fund makes bond and note payments for the General Fund and other funds, with money they send it, so a fall here is not a cut to a service. Two votes the Board took in 2026 paid debt down, mostly with savings:

  • Resolution 2026-642 (July 7, 2026, unanimous) pays down the 2018 Series B refunding bonds with $7,212,941 of Community Preservation Fund balance and $92,059 from the sale of Town property.
  • Resolution 2026-762 (August 4, 2026, unanimous) pays down the Town Square bond anticipation note with $1,874,218 of General Fund balance and $122,500 of rent from the Town Square properties.

In the 2027 Preliminary, the Community Preservation Fund sends the Debt Service Fund nothing; the 2026 budget had it send $2,959,300. That fund's own budget does not shrink: a new line, “Fund Balance Contribution”, adds the same $2,959,300 to its savings instead, which is why the Community Preservation Fund is not flagged.

All five revenue lines the 2027 Preliminary raises are still at or below what the Town collected in 2025, so the increases follow results the Town has already seen. Summer Rec Camp is a new line, with no adopted budget or 2025 figure to compare.

A big move in one line is not a problem in itself. Some are a line renamed or moved to another account, some are a new contract, and some are a closer estimate of what the Town really collects. Each is a place to ask a question.

Recurring costs by category

The flags above follow funds, and budget accuracy follows single lines. This puts the lines back together by the kind of cost they are, across every fund, so a flagged line can be read against its own history: a pattern, or a single event. Spending is from 2018, budgets from 2019, using the Town’s own account codes.

This is governmental accounting. The Town records each of these as an expenditure of the fund that pays it, by function (the department) and object (what was bought), under the State Comptroller’s chart of accounts. Each budget line is an appropriation, a legal limit on spending: money left over lapses into fund balance, and spending past the limit needs a budget transfer. The “kind of cost” note on each category (fixed, variable, semi-variable) is a budgeting term for what makes it move and what the Town can change; it is not a category in the Town’s books.

Original, not amended, budgets. Every “budget” here is the budget as the Board first adopted it, which is what the Supplements print. During the year the Board amends it: adjustments add money from a grant, a donation or savings, and transfers move it between lines. A line that looks over its original budget may have been covered by such a vote, and one that looks under may have given money to another line. Under each account, this lists the Board’s 2026 budget changes that name it, from the records through November 5, 2026; read the resolution for which way the money moved. Not every fiscal impact statement lists its accounts, so these lists can be incomplete.

Electricity2025: $3,243,148 spent of $3,231,000 budgeted; 2026 likely $3,940,000 to $4,470,000 against $3,339,648, over budget.

Power for Town buildings, the water and sewer plants, pump stations and street lights. 13 accounts.

Kind of cost: semi-variable. What moves it: a monthly service charge, plus the power used, which rises with the water pumped, the sewage treated, the buildings open and the street lights lit, times the utility’s rate.

What the Town controls: The rate is set by the utility and its regulators, not the Town. How much power is used is the Town’s to manage: equipment, buildings and lighting.

  • Spending came in under the budget in 4 of 7 years (2019–2025) and over it in 3. Over the last five years it averaged $3,353 a year below budget.
  • Spending rose 33% from 2019 to 2025; the 2026 budget is 26% above 2019’s.
  • By June 30, 2026: $1,355,493, 22% more than by the same date in 2025. If the rest of the year follows 2025’s timing, it ends near $3,940,000, $600,000 over the $3,339,648 budget. Across the last 4 years, 30% to 34% of the year’s spending came by June 30, which puts 2026 between $3,940,000 and $4,470,000, all of it over budget. These are this site’s estimates.
  • The 2027 Preliminary budgets $3,516,141, $272,993 above what was spent in 2025.
  • 1 of its accounts is named in 2026 budget changes the Board adopted, listed under each account below, in the records through November 5, 2026.

Heating fuel and gas2025: $164,002 spent of $216,200 budgeted; 2026 likely $180,000 to $210,000 against $225,400.

Heating oil and natural gas for Town buildings and plants. 6 accounts.

Kind of cost: semi-variable. What moves it: mostly the weather (how cold the winter is), times the price of oil or gas, with a smaller steady base for the plants.

What the Town controls: The price and the weather are outside the Town’s control; insulation, boilers and thermostats are within it.

  • Spending came in under the budget in 7 of 7 years (2019–2025) and over it in 0. Over the last five years it averaged $42,850 a year below budget.
  • Spending rose 64% from 2019 to 2025; the 2026 budget is 25% above 2019’s.
  • By June 30, 2026: $123,334, 23% more than by the same date in 2025. If the rest of the year follows 2025’s timing, it ends near $200,000, within the $225,400 budget. Across the last 4 years, 59% to 69% of the year’s spending came by June 30, which puts 2026 between $180,000 and $210,000, within budget. These are this site’s estimates.
  • The 2027 Preliminary budgets $245,000, $80,998 above what was spent in 2025.
  • No 2026 budget change the Board adopted names an account in this category, in the records through November 5, 2026.

What the Town controls: The price is not the Town’s to set; the size of the fleet, the vehicles bought and how they are used are.

Supplies2025: $1,060,990 spent of $1,324,210 budgeted; 2026 likely $1,020,000 to $1,200,000 against $1,383,915.

Office, program, computer and operating supplies, including the water and sewer plants’ chemicals. 108 accounts.

Kind of cost: mixed, partly variable and partly fixed. What moves it: the plants’ chemicals vary with the water and sewage treated and the treatment rules; office and program supplies stay close to the same each year.

What the Town controls: Largely within departments’ control, except chemicals the treatment standards require.

  • Spending came in under the budget in 5 of 7 years (2019–2025) and over it in 2. Over the last five years it averaged $53,321 a year below budget.
  • Spending rose 58% from 2019 to 2025; the 2026 budget is 56% above 2019’s.
  • By June 30, 2026: $404,805, 5% more than by the same date in 2025. If the rest of the year follows 2025’s timing, it ends near $1,110,000, within the $1,383,915 budget. Across the last 4 years, 34% to 40% of the year’s spending came by June 30, which puts 2026 between $1,020,000 and $1,200,000, within budget. These are this site’s estimates.
  • The 2027 Preliminary budgets $1,423,840, $362,850 above what was spent in 2025.
  • 5 of its accounts are named in 2026 budget changes the Board adopted, listed under each account below, in the records through November 5, 2026.
  • 9 accounts in this category are flagged on budget accuracy.

Mailing, including tax bills and water bills. 8 accounts.

Kind of cost: fixed. What moves it: mostly the same mailings each year to the same property owners and water customers, so it moves mainly when postal rates rise.

What the Town controls: Postal rates are set by the Postal Service; the number of mailings, and moving bills to email, are the Town’s choice.

  • Spending came in under the budget in 7 of 7 years (2019–2025) and over it in 0. Over the last five years it averaged $10,888 a year below budget.
  • Spending rose 10% from 2019 to 2025; the 2026 budget is 20% above 2019’s.
  • By June 30, 2026: $64,470, 26% less than by the same date in 2025. The share spent by June 30 varies too much from year to year for a single figure. Across the last 4 years, 73% to 89% of the year’s spending came by June 30, which puts 2026 between $70,000 and $90,000, within budget. These are this site’s estimates.
  • The 2027 Preliminary budgets $117,515, $18,793 above what was spent in 2025.
  • No 2026 budget change the Board adopted names an account in this category, in the records through November 5, 2026.

Costs the Town codes as miscellaneous, including bank fees. 21 accounts.

Kind of cost: none in particular, a catch-all. What moves it: whatever the Town codes as miscellaneous, so it has no single driver; a large entry here is a reason to ask what it was.

What the Town controls: Within the Town’s control, case by case.

  • Spending came in under the budget in 3 of 7 years (2019–2025) and over it in 4. Over the last five years it averaged $10,609 a year above budget.
  • Spending fell 26% from 2019 to 2025; the 2026 budget is 7% below 2019’s.
  • By June 30, 2026: $87,499, 135% more than by the same date in 2025. If the rest of the year follows 2025’s timing, it ends near $210,000, $70,000 over the $144,449 budget. Across the last 4 years, 42% to 45% of the year’s spending came by June 30, which puts 2026 between $190,000 and $210,000, all of it over budget. These are this site’s estimates.
  • The 2027 Preliminary budgets $95,122, $5,507 above what was spent in 2025.
  • One entry is left out of the figures above: “Water - Miscellaneous” (EW1-8-8320-490-000-00000) recorded $3,580,426 in 2025 against an original budget of $7,000, on page 45 of the Supplement. A federal grant for a water-main extension that passes through the Water District’s books. The Board amended the 2025 budget in July 2026, after the year had ended, moving $3,575,000 from Federal Aid to this line. The line’s 2025 spending, $3,580,426, is that amount plus about $5,400, close to its usual few thousand dollars a year. The resolution, 2026-640 of July 7, 2026 (“Suffolk County Water Authority Federal Pass-Through Grant 2025 Budget Adjustment”), says “the Town was notified that it would receive approximately $3.5 Million dollars of pass-through grant” and “congressionally mandated project, known as Extension 94, with final awards of $2,275,000 for 2022 and $1,300,000 for 2023”.
  • 2 of its accounts are named in 2026 budget changes the Board adopted, listed under each account below, in the records through November 5, 2026.

Cleaning allowance2025: $169,106 spent of $173,100 budgeted.

The yearly clothing-cleaning payment union contracts give employees, mostly police officers. It is pay, coded as Personal Services. 29 accounts.

Kind of cost: fixed. What moves it: an amount per employee set in each union contract, so the total moves with the number of eligible employees and with each new contract.

What the Town controls: Not controllable during a contract; it is set when the Town negotiates the next one.

  • Spending came in under the budget in 5 of 7 years (2019–2025) and over it in 2. Over the last five years it averaged $1,384 a year above budget.

  • Nothing is recorded by June 30 in either year: it is paid later in the year.
  • The 2027 Preliminary budgets $171,800, $2,694 above what was spent in 2025.

A category is the set of accounts with its object codes, in every fund. “Spent by June 30” is the Supplement’s year-to-date column. Projections for 2026 are this site’s estimates: a range from the share of each recent year’s spending that came by June 30, and a single figure only where that share has held within 15 points. These are likely questions for residents, not findings.

Patterns across funds

The lists above find single lines that moved. This section looks at each fund as a whole, every year from 2018 to 2025: what it collected against its revenue estimate, what it spent against its budget, and a least-squares trend line through each. Four patterns repeat across funds. They are questions worth asking, not findings that anything was done wrong.

Revenue estimates run low

The General Fund collected more than it estimated in every year from 2021 to 2025, by $4.23 million a year on average over those 5 years (+5.1% of the estimate over all 7 years since 2019). The largest gains were interest and earnings ($749,193 a year), state aid for mortgage tax ($480,466 a year), building inspection fees ($253,440 a year) and sales tax ($250,541 a year). The 2024 and 2025 budgets each planned to use savings ($2.00 million and $1.75 million of appropriated fund balance), yet on the Supplements’ figures the fund collected $3.17 million and $5.44 million more than it spent in those years ($0.76 million and $4.44 million after its transfers to capital projects).

Water District (6 of 7 years, +25.7%), Community Preservation Fund (7 of 7 years, +100.3%), Riverhead Scavenger Waste (7 of 7 years, +24.7%) and Street Lighting District (6 of 7 years, +23.9%) also collected more than estimated in most years. Cautious revenue estimates are sound practice, but estimates that run low every year build a cushion the budget does not show, and can lead to taxes or rents set higher than needed. See Revenue for each line.

Capital paid for with transfers the budget did not plan

Money moved from operating funds to capital project funds (H01, and the districts’ project funds EW3, ES2, ES4 and ES6) almost never appears in the adopted budget. It is added during the year. Net of reversals, the Water District sent $11.4 million, the General Fund sent $5.01 million, the Calverton Sewer District sent $3.47 million, the Street Lighting District sent $1.03 million, the Riverhead Sewer District sent $0.37 million, Riverhead Scavenger Waste sent $0.34 million and the Community Preservation Fund sent $0.34 million this way from 2018 to 2025. The largest were $7.75 million from the Water District in 2024, $3.49 million from the Water District in 2025, $2.41 million from the General Fund in 2024, $7.65 million from the Calverton Sewer District in 2020 ($4.18 million of it returned in 2021) and $1.00 million from the Street Lighting District in 2019.

Paying for capital in cash rather than borrowing saves interest. But when it is decided mid-year, the adopted budget understates what a fund will spend, and the decision gets less public review than the budget does. Planning these transfers in the budget, or in a multi-year capital plan, would show them in advance. See Capital and debt.

In the utility districts, “fund balance” offsets depreciation

In the Water District (2019 to 2025), the Riverhead Sewer District (2019 to 2025), Riverhead Scavenger Waste (2019 to 2025) and the Calverton Sewer District (2019 to 2025), the appropriated fund balance in the adopted budget equals the depreciation budget to the dollar. These districts keep business-style books on the full accrual basis, so they record depreciation, the cost of their plant wearing out, as an expense. It uses no cash. A budget that lists the same amount as “appropriated fund balance” is balancing that non-cash expense, not drawing down savings.

With depreciation and other non-cash entries set aside, these districts collected more than they spent in most years: the Water District in 8 of 8, the Riverhead Sewer District in 6 of 8, Riverhead Scavenger Waste in 8 of 8 and the Calverton Sewer District in 7 of 8. The records do not say why the two figures are set equal; the match in every year suggests it is the Town’s practice. A reader adding up “fund balance used” across funds should leave these out.

Spending growing faster than collections

In the Ambulance District, spending has grown about +4.7% a year on its trend line, collections about +2.0%. The fund went from collecting $238,715 more than it spent in 2019 to spending $106,958 more than it collected in 2025, short in each of the last three years. Its budgets have also counted on ambulance billing the district has not collected; see Revenue.

How this is computed. Collected is every revenue line but appropriated fund balance, transfers in from other funds included. Spent is every spending line less non-cash entries (depreciation, losses on disposing of assets, pension expense under GASB 68), less transfers to capital project funds (shown separately above), and less the 2025 Water District grant explained by Resolution 2026-640. Budgets are the original adopted ones; the Board amends them during the year. Funds spending under $200,000 and the Debt Service Fund, which only passes payments through, are left out. With eight years of data a trend line is a rough guide, and the Supplements’ figures can differ from the audited statements.

Independent public-records guide for Riverhead residents.

Riverhead Budget Live is an independent project. It is not run, approved, or endorsed by the Town of Riverhead. The site organizes public information and provides analysis; it is not a substitute for the Town’s official records. Check the linked source documents before relying on an important figure. Basic, aggregated site-usage statistics are collected through Google Analytics. You do not need an account to use this site. There are no ads.
